tagline: Where great rivers meet the sea
overview:
Bangladesh is a low, green land built by rivers. The mighty Ganges (called the Padma here), the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) and the Meghna flow down from the Himalayas and spread into the largest river delta on Earth before reaching the Bay of Bengal. India wraps around the country on three sides, with a short border with Myanmar in the southeast.

Although it is only about 147,600 km², roughly the size of the US state of Iowa, Bangladesh is home to about 170 million people, making it one of the most crowded countries in the world. Nearly everyone speaks Bengali, also called Bangla, and most people are Muslim. The capital, Dhaka, is a city of some 20 million, famous for its swarms of colorful bicycle rickshaws.

Bangladesh is a parliamentary republic. Farming rice and jute remains important, but the country has become the world's second-largest maker of clothing, and its economy has grown fast in recent decades despite the constant challenge of floods and cyclones.
landAndNature:
Most of Bangladesh lies less than 10 meters above sea level, a vast floodplain of rice paddies crisscrossed by hundreds of rivers. Every summer the monsoon rains and melting Himalayan snow swell the rivers, and about a fifth of the country floods, leaving behind rich soil. Cyclones spinning up from the Bay of Bengal can drive seawater far inland. Only in the southeast, around Chittagong and the Hill Tracts, does the land rise into forested hills.

In the southwest, the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, spread across the delta into India. Bengal tigers prowl its muddy islands, sharing them with saltwater crocodiles, spotted deer and river dolphins. Cox's Bazar, on the southeast coast, has a sandy beach that stretches unbroken for about 120 kilometers.
peopleAndCulture:
Bengali is spoken by almost everyone, and Bangladeshis are so proud of it that students who died in 1952 protesting for the right to use their language are honored every February 21, now marked worldwide as International Mother Language Day. Rice and fish are eaten at nearly every meal; the silvery hilsa is the national fish, and mustard oil, chilies and lentils flavor the cooking. Sweets made from milk, such as mishti doi and roshogolla, end a meal.

Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year in April, fills the streets with processions, masks and music. Poetry and song are treasured; the poet Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthem. Cricket is the most popular sport, and kabaddi, a team tag-and-wrestling game, is the traditional national sport. Fine jamdani muslin weaving is a craft recognized by UNESCO.
history:
Bengal has been a rich land of farmers and traders for thousands of years, ruled by Buddhist and Hindu kingdoms such as the Pala dynasty and, from the 1200s, by Muslim sultans and later the Mughal emperors. Its fine cotton cloth was famous as far away as Rome. In 1757 the British East India Company defeated the ruler of Bengal at Plassey, and the region became the heart of British India for nearly two centuries, suffering terrible famines under colonial rule.

When India and Pakistan were divided in 1947, this mostly Muslim region became East Pakistan, separated from West Pakistan by 1,600 kilometers of India. Bengalis grew angry at being treated as second-class, and after Pakistan's army launched a brutal crackdown in March 1971, a nine-month war of independence followed. With India's help, Bangladesh won its freedom on December 16, 1971, led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
funFacts: Dhaka is called the rickshaw capital of the world, with hundreds of thousands of hand-painted cycle rickshaws on its streets.
Bangladesh is the world's second-largest exporter of clothing; a huge share of the T-shirts sold worldwide are sewn there.
The Sundarbans is the only mangrove forest on Earth where tigers live, and they are strong swimmers.
The national anthem was written by Rabindranath Tagore, who also wrote India's anthem; he is the only person to have written two.
Cox's Bazar beach runs about 120 kilometers, one of the longest natural sandy beaches in the world.
Bangladesh has about 700 rivers, and boats carry more passengers than trains in many regions.
